transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-02
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Marcus Chen (EchoCare CTO), Leah Alvarez (EchoCare Lead ML Eng), Naveen Patel (EchoCare DevOps)

Summary: Quick model catalog walkthrough focused on selecting open models for EchoCare's chat summarization/provide assistant, discussion of benchmarks (latency, qual, cost), and compatibility matrix for on-prem/dedicated/private deployment options. Agreed to run benchmarks on EchoCare prompts and follow up with POC scoping.

Topics: model selection, quantization, batching, latency vs cost, VPC/private deployment requirements, SOC2/KMS, compatibility matrix, trial API keys, next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time today. Uh, quick intro - I'm Jordan, AE, and with me is Priya, our SE. We're gonna run through the model catalog, benchmarks, and the compatibility matrix for EchoCare's use case.
[00:18] Marcus Chen: Thanks Jordan. Quick context - we're evaluating options to replace our in-house summarization infra, and want to understand if Redwood's hosted API or Dedicated pool makes sense. We have PHI-ish metadata and some de-identifiable notes, so security is huge.
[00:34] Priya Raman: Totally. We'll cover Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private and how the catalog maps to those modes. Also show Console and Optimize recommendations - batching, quant profiles.
[00:50] Leah Alvarez: Our primary metrics are latency under 600ms p95 for short summaries, and inference cost per 1k tokens. Also model quality on domain prompts - we have a few sample prompt sets we'll share.
[01:06] Naveen Patel: And network constraints: EchoCare requires VPC peering for Private deployment or we might do an on-prem package. We use Okta SSO, KMS with AWS CloudHSM, and strict audit logs.
[01:24] Jordan Lee: Great - that maps to the usual enterprise checklist. We'll point to our SOC 2 docs and the Private deployment KMS patterns.
[01:40] [01:40] Jordan Lee: Alright jump into the model catalog screen - I'm sharing a deck plus a spreadsheet link: https://redwood.example.com/decks/model-catalog-echo.
[02:05] Priya Raman: On the left column you can see curated open models we publish - smaller Llama variants, BLOOM, Mistral-style weights, plus Redwood-verified performance rows. Compatibility flags indicate CPU/GPU, quantization support (4-bit,8-bit), and recommended batch sizes.
[02:35] Marcus Chen: How accurate are the performance numbers? Are they racked on our sequences?
[02:45] Priya Raman: They are host benchmarks on standard eval prompts but we do recommend running a short benchmark with your prompts - the Console has a bench harness that will run your prompt set across model candidates and produce p50/p95 latency and cost.
[03:05] Leah Alvarez: Nice. Is that the same spreadsheet you mentioned?
[03:12] Priya Raman: Yes - here's the compatibility matrix CSV export link in the Console - it shows kernel support, KV cache behavior, whether the model supports continuous batching, and which sequence lengths it's optimized for. Example row: llama-2-13b-q4: Supported on A100/RTX, 4bit quant OK, good for seq <=1024.
[03:36] Marcus Chen: We have two main workflows: short note summarization (avg 200 tokens) and longer patient narrative distillations (avg 1500 tokens). Any models you'd recommend?
[03:50] Priya Raman: For 200-token summaries, smaller quantized 7b-13b variants often hit your latency/cost sweet spot. For 1500-token, you'd look at 13b+ models with attention kernel optimizations - and possibly a CPU+GPU split or streaming. We can recommend dynamic batching and prefix KV caching to reduce token compute for repeated context.
[04:16] [04:16] Marcus Chen: What about hallucination/regulatory concerns for clinical text?
[04:24] Jordan Lee: Important question - we recommend model evaluation via our evaluation harness: you can run rouge/bleu style metrics and custom rubric checks. For clinical reliability, best practice is a smaller model with domain-tuned prompts + reranking or a safety pass. We also support tool-calling patterns to validate extractions against canonical patient data.
[04:53] Leah Alvarez: Do you support fine-tuning or instruction-tuning in the hosted offering?
[04:59] Priya Raman: Hosted supports prompts/adapter style tuning via Redwood Optimize recommendations; dedicated/private can be provisioned for fine-tuning workflows depending on contract. We'll map options in the compatibility matrix.
[05:18] [05:18] Naveen Patel: From a deployment perspective: if we choose Dedicated, can we attach our KMS?
[05:24] Jordan Lee: Yes, Dedicated and Private let you bring your KMS - we have integrations for AWS KMS, CloudHSM, and HSM workflows. We'll share the configuration guide.
[05:36] [06:00] Priya Raman: I'm going to show the benchmark tab - here's a sample run (note: numbers are noisy): llama-7b-q4 => p50 ~120ms, p95 ~420ms on a batch size 1 on an RTX A10G; cost per 1k tokens $0.18. For larger models like 13b quant it's p50 220ms p95 650ms and cost $0.45 per 1k. These are illustrative.
[06:30] Marcus Chen: That p95 for 13b is slightly above our 600ms target for long flows. Could we tune batching or sequence chunking to improve it?
[06:40] Priya Raman: Yes, you can reduce p95 by kernel selection (we pick fused attention kernels), enable early stopping in streaming, and optimize batching for tail latency. Also Redwood Optimize can recommend a quant profile to reduce FP compute while preserving quality.
[07:02] [07:02] Leah Alvarez: How are model compatibility flags generated? Sometimes we see mismatched labels in other platforms.
[07:10] Priya Raman: Good callout - we run a compatibility test suite per model: kernel checks, quantization pass, context-length stress tests, and a simple inference smoke test. We try to keep it accurate but edge cases happen - hence the export to run your own bench.
[07:30] Marcus Chen: Are there any known gaps for models trained with Alibi or special attention?
[07:36] Priya Raman: Occasionally certain attention implementations need custom kernels. The matrix flags those as "custom kernel required". If you need a model with that, our private runtime can load custom kernels as part of onboarding.
[07:52] [08:00] Jordan Lee: Switching to the Console: the Optimize tab will show recommended batch size and a quant profile for each route. You can set route-level SLOs (latency vs cost) - the router will pick a model variant that fits and will fallback if capacity constrained.
[08:26] Leah Alvarez: That fallback behavior - is it deterministic? We don't want silent degradation in production.
[08:33] Jordan Lee: Fallbacks are policy-driven and logged in the Console. You can set hard fallbacks to block requests or soft fallbacks that route to a cheaper model and flag the response. We also emit trace logs for each decision.
[08:52] Naveen Patel: What about audit logs for PHI? Retention, export?
[09:00] Priya Raman: We have per-tenant audit logs with retention controls - Dedicated and Private let you control retention and export to your SIEM. Hosted can stream logs to S3 or your logging endpoints; encryption at rest and in transit with KMS.
[09:18] [09:18] Marcus Chen: Ok, re: cost - if we run 100M tokens a month, what's the delta between hosted and dedicated?
[09:26] Jordan Lee: Rough ballpark: hosted is pay-as-you-go; dedicated is reserved capacity with better unit economics for sustained throughput. We can model it for your expected token mix and show a cost comparison in the spreadsheet.
[09:42] Marcus Chen: Great, that's important for procurement.
[09:48] [10:00] Priya Raman: I'm going to demo an export: here's the bench results for a sample prompt set - you can see per-model quality metrics and per-route recommended quant. We'll attach that as a CSV after the call.
[10:25] Leah Alvarez: For our long sequences, do you recommend a specific memory strategy? We worry about OOMs if we mischoose quant or kernel.
[10:34] Priya Raman: Use attention windowing plus KV cache eviction; for very long sequences we recommend offloading KV to NVMe on Dedicated or Private. The compatibility matrix tags models that handle cache offload properly.
[10:55] [11:00] Marcus Chen: Regulatory: we need SOC2 plus penetration testing attestation. Can you provide that?
[11:07] Jordan Lee: Yes - we'll share SOC2 Type II and pen test summary. For Private and Dedicated we can provide more granular evidence.
[11:18] [11:18] Naveen Patel: Any customers in healthcare you can point to?
[11:24] Jordan Lee: We have a few anonymized case studies - will share references in the follow-up.
[11:32] [12:00] Priya Raman: Quick Q on prompt engineering: sharing your sample prompts helps us build a more realistic benchmark. Leah, you mentioned you'd share those?
[12:08] Leah Alvarez: Yes, I'll export a sanitized set by end of day tomorrow.
[12:14] Marcus Chen: Timeline - we want to pick a vendor by end of month and start POC mid-March.
[12:22] Jordan Lee: Sounds reasonable. Next steps: we'll send the compatibility matrix, benchmark harness link, pricing, and SOC2 docs. Also provision trial keys.
[12:36] [13:00] Priya Raman: I'm going to call out a few model candidates by use-case: short summaries => llama-7b-q4, mistral-x-7b-q4; long narratives => llama-13b-8bit, m-13b-fused. We'll mark which need custom kernels.
[13:22] Marcus Chen: For privacy, would you recommend hosted with de-id plus SSO, or go straight to Dedicated/Private?
[13:30] Jordan Lee: If your workload includes PHI, most customers opt for Dedicated as a middle ground - you get reserved capacity and customer-managed keys. Private is for on-prem/air-gap regulatory needs. We can layout a migration path.
[13:46] [14:00] Leah Alvarez: Anything else on the compatibility matrix we should watch for?
[14:07] Priya Raman: Check sequence length columns, kernel flags, and quantization notes. Also runtime caveats like memory offload and streaming behaviors.
[14:22] [15:00] Jordan Lee: Ok I'll summarize - action items: Jordan will send pricing and benchmark spreadsheet; Priya will produce the compatibility matrix with suggested model variants; Leah will provide sanitized prompts; we'll schedule POC scoping for week of Mar 9.
[15:36] Marcus Chen: Sounds good. One minor question - do you support direct database lookups as a tool call for verification?
[15:44] Priya Raman: Yes, tool-calling is supported with secure connectors; we recommend placing verification steps in a separate transaction to avoid PHI leakage. We'll share patterns.
[16:02] [16:00] Naveen Patel: Ok thanks, this was useful.
[16:06] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and schedule.

End of transcript.
